# Understand app permissions

Apps are third-party services that you can connect with your Slack workspace. Each app has a unique set of [permission scopes](https://api.slack.com/scopes) that tell you what information the app can access in Slack and how it can use that information. Use this guide to better understand app permissions and how to evaluate them.

## App permissions overview

An app’s scopes depend on the kinds of things it was built to do. Generally, apps can do three things in Slack:

- View information
- Post information
- Perform actions

**Note:** We recommend only choosing tools and services you trust when installing apps to Slack. Before adding an app, you can review its privacy policy from the app page in the Slack Marketplace.

## Evaluate app permissions

There are two things you should consider when evaluating an app's permissions:

- What information the app will have access to in Slack, such as member profiles, channel names, messages, or files.
- What the app can do with the information it can access, like post messages, modify content, or create channels.

### Installed apps

If an app is already installed to your workspace, search for it from the **Installed apps** tab on [your workspace's Apps page](https://app.slack.com/apps-manage) in the Slack Marketplace to see who installed it and what information the app can access.

### New apps

Before you [install an app](https://slack.com/help/articles/202035138-Add-apps-to-your-Slack-workspace#install-apps) or [approve an app installation request](https://slack.com/help/articles/222386767-Manage-app-approval-for-your-workspace#review-app-requests), you'll see a full list of permissions the app is requesting, including what information it can view and what actions it can take in your workspace.

Apps can take actions on behalf of a user or on behalf of the app. For example, an app may request permission to access messages in channels a user belongs to or post messages on their behalf. Apps can also take actions independently of users, like adding [slash commands](https://slack.com/help/articles/201259356) or posting messages as the app.

![Google Calendar app permissions showing data the app can access in Slack](https://slack.zendesk.com/hc/article_attachments/32816748180499)

### Bots

Some apps create [bot users](https://api.slack.com/bot-users) in Slack. Bots can access the same information as workspace members, and may be able to take the same actions that members can.

If an app you're installing requests the [**bot** scope](https://api.slack.com/scopes/bot), that means it's an older app that may have access to a wide range of actions and information in Slack. Newer apps will request a narrower set of scopes that allow bots access to specific actions and information, regardless of whether an app has updated its bot user or not.

![Google Calendar app permissions showing actions the app can take in Slack](https://slack.zendesk.com/hc/article_attachments/32816748181011)

### Agents

Some apps run as agents that can autonomously take actions in Slack on your behalf. Like bots, agents may be able to read messages, post updates, join channels, and interact with other apps. Unlike bots, agents can make multi-step decisions and carry out complex tasks based on goals you or your admin define.

Agent permissions are based on the scopes permitted for the app and aren’t affected by any [restrictions on native Slack AI](https://slack.com/help/articles/28244420881555-Manage-access-to-AI-features-in-Slack).

## View access types

Access types help you understand the kind of information an app can view in Slack. Workspace Owners and Admins can filter apps by access type from the **Approved apps**, **Restricted apps**, or **Installed apps** tabs on the [Apps page](https://app.slack.com/marketplace-manage) in the Slack Marketplace:

1. Click your **workspace name** in the sidebar.

![](https://a.slack-edge.com/8e8e4/helpcenter/img/workspace-picker@2x.jpg)
2. Hover over **Tools & settings**.
3. Select **Settings & administration** from the menu, then click **Manage apps** to open the Slack Marketplace.
4. Click **Installed Apps** at the top of the left sidebar.
5. Click the drop-down menu below **Access types** to view apps with different access types.
